title: Chapter 35 – Outer Court
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Feng]

The Hundred-Stair Gate of the Azure Cloud Sect is not a gate at all. It is a wall of weathered white stone, thirty feet high, with a long stair cut into the face of it, and above the stair, very far above, a pale bank of cloud that never seems to move.

Lin Feng stands at the bottom with his spear on his back and a cloth bundle in his left hand, and he is trying not to look as if he is trying not to look up.

He has walked for nine days. Six of them from Willow Ford, in a line of tributary-house youths led by a sour Sect courier on a gray horse, and three more up the long mountain road to the Outer Court. Forty-one boys and girls, between thirteen and seventeen. Every one of them is the pick of a house. Every one of them has been told that they are the pride of their family, that the future of the clan rests on their shoulders, and that they must not, under any circumstances, embarrass anyone. He has not heard a single one of them say it aloud. He has seen it on all their faces.

A boy from a river house beside him is sick on the cobbles.

"Do not look at the top," Feng tells him. "Look at the next step."

"I am looking at the next step."

"Then why are you sick?"

"Because I can see all the next steps."

Feng laughs, once, quietly. It is the first time he has laughed in two weeks. It surprises him how good it feels.

He is sixteen. He is taller than most of the boys around him, and heavier in the shoulder, and he carries himself like what he is, the heir to a clan that is dying and does not mean to. His tunic is the plain gray of a Lin household junior. His spear is ash and spirit iron. Down the back of his neck, tied with a bit of green cord, hangs a short bamboo tube that he has not opened since he left home.

In it is a talisman. It was pressed into his hand on the last night by a ten-year-old boy who looked at him with serious dark eyes and said: Do not use it unless you really need to.

Which means, Feng thinks, that I will probably need to by noon.

* * *

"Lin," says a cool voice behind him. "From the hill that is going cold."

Feng turns. A boy of fourteen stands there in a river-green tunic with the Red Ridge crest at the collar, slight and fair, with a soft face and very hard eyes. He is flanked by two others in the same green. One of them is chewing a stalk of grass.

"Zhao Yao," the boy says, as if the name were a title. "My cousin Qian wrote to say you would be here. He asked me to look after you." The smile is thin and perfectly polite. "He said you would need it."

"I do not need looking after."

"Everyone needs it in the Outer Court." Yao tilts his head. "The stair is a long way. Some say it is longer for a house that cannot pay its tribute without selling slag. I would hate for you to fall. It would be such a pity for the heir to disappear on his first day."

Disappear. Feng's hand tightens on the strap of his spear. It is a careless word, he tells himself, the kind of word a boy of fourteen uses to hurt. But the boy with the grass in his mouth stops chewing, very slightly, and looks away.

"I will not fall," Feng says.

"I am sure you will not." Yao steps close, and lowers his voice. "My uncle asked me to tell you something else. He said that your hill has a very clever little pig on it, and that he would like to meet him. He said it was a courtesy." The soft face does not change. "What does he mean?"

Feng looks at him for a long moment. He is thinking of a boy with a plum in his fist and a face like still water. He is thinking of a promise made in a green dusk, with a hard hand on a small head.

"I have a brother," he says, very evenly, "who is ten. He counts things. He is slow. He is not clever. If your uncle wishes to meet him, he may come to the hill and meet him like a neighbor, in daylight, at the front gate." He lets a breath out. "If anyone comes to meet him some other way, I will find them. I do not care how long it takes."

For an instant the soft face goes blank, as though a hand has been wiped across a slate. Then Yao laughs, lightly, and steps back.

"What a loyal brother," he says. "I will tell my uncle."

He goes. The boy with the grass follows, and looks back once, a quick sideways glance that Feng cannot read.

Feng stands with his heart going hard. Qian wrote ahead. Heng told him to say it. They want me to carry it home like a letter. He turns it over for a long minute, and does not like any side of it. Then he picks up his bundle, and finds a place in the line, and does not look at the Zhao boys again.

The Gate Trial begins at the second bell.

It is, the courier explains to the line of nervous children, very simple. The stair has a hundred steps. Each step carries a little more pressure than the last, a Sect array laid into the stone by the founders to test the Qi and the will of anyone who climbs. At the fortieth step an ordinary Qi Refining cultivator begins to feel it. At the seventieth, only the strong are still moving. At the hundredth, according to the Sect's own records, it equals the pressure of a Qi Refining ninth-stage at full strength. Nobody in the last fifty years has reached the top in their first attempt.

Anyone who passes the fortieth step enters the Outer Court as a junior disciple. Anyone who passes the sixtieth enters as a named disciple, with a stipend and a teacher. And anyone who passes the eightieth, the courier says with a thin little smile, will be remembered.

"Those who cannot continue need only stop," he says. "Do not struggle against the array. It will lift you gently from the stair. There is no shame in being lifted."

Feng looks at the boy beside him. The boy has gone green.

"Go slowly," Feng says. "Breathe from the belly. Keep your weight over your feet."

"You are not even nervous."

"I am terrified." Feng shrugs. "I am just more used to it."

They climb in groups of five. He is in the third. The first group goes up and comes down again in a quarter of an hour, one at a time, carried in the arms of invisible hands, and a black-robed attendant at the foot of the stair writes each name on a board with a number. Thirty-one. Twenty-eight. Forty-two. A girl in a flame-colored cloak reaches fifty-five and stands there swaying for a long minute before the array lifts her gently away, and she looks furious.

Then it is his turn.

He steps onto the first stair. Nothing happens.

Easy, he thinks. Of course it is easy. It is meant to be easy at the start.

By the tenth step, a faint weight lies on his shoulders like a damp cloak. By the twentieth it presses on his chest. By the thirtieth he is breathing through his teeth, and the Qi in his channels has begun to run thick and sluggish, like honey in winter. He knows the feeling. It is exactly the weight of Grandfather's presence on the wall, the day he was eleven and had to stand beside the old man in a spear form and could not move his arms.

Forty. The fortieth step is cold under his sandals. He passes it, and a white mark glimmers on the stone at his heel.

He keeps walking.

Fifty. The array no longer pushes. It presses, and the pressure has a voice, a thin high note just beyond hearing that sets his teeth on edge. His spear on his back has become a ton of iron. His left leg, below the knee, has begun to ache.

Sixty. A second white mark. His vision goes narrow. He sees a single stone and the edge of the next.

Somewhere far below, a voice calls out something that sounds like his name.

He does not stop. He has not been taught how to stop. The first thing Grandfather ever taught him with a spear was not a form. It was how to stand when everything in his body begged him to fall. Hold the hill, the old man had said, and Feng did not understand it until the night of the ring. Now it is as clear as water. The stair is only a very long hill.

Seventy. The pressure becomes pain. Qi surges up through him in a wild green-red-brown tangle, wood and fire and earth all rushing at once, and the three roots of his body, the gift that makes him rare and the burden that makes him slow, seize and strain against each other.

Seventy-one. Seventy-two.

The ache in his left leg turns into a burn.

It is the same burn. He knows it at once. It is not the pressure of the array. It is a thin, cold line below the knee, a thread under the skin, where a man in a red mist once laid a finger against him on a cold winter day and said nothing. Jian cleaned it out, he had been told. He had been told it was gone. He had walked on it for two years, and run on it, and danced on it with a spear.

Not now.

Seventy-three.

All at once a spot of red light flashes on the stair beneath his left foot, a small bright glyph that has not appeared for any of the other children. It spreads under him, a ring of crimson fire in the white stone. A bell rings, sharply and clearly, from somewhere above.

The array stops.

It does not lift him. It simply stops, the pressure draining away so suddenly that he staggers and has to catch his weight on the spear. He stands in the center of the red ring with his chest heaving and sweat running into his eyes, and he looks up the stair, and a man in a plain gray robe is coming down toward him with an unhurried tread.

* * *

The man is not old. Thirty-five, perhaps, or forty, with a thin, lined, clever face and a head of untidy black hair held back by a wooden pin. He wears the plain robe of an Outer Affairs inspector, with the three-cloud crest on the breast. There is a smear of ink on his thumb. He looks like a clerk who has been interrupted at his dinner.

He stops two steps above Feng and examines the glyph under his feet with every sign of professional interest.

"Blood Qi," he says. "Faint. Old. Very well hidden." He looks up. "Do you know what you have on your left leg, young man?"

"Yes," Feng says. He is not sure his voice will hold. "A Blood Shadow rogue touched it, two winters ago. My brother cleaned it out. They said it was gone."

"Your brother cleaned it out."

"With a poultice. And our aunt's herbs."

"I see." The inspector's gaze lingers on him a moment. It is mild and curious and wholly without hostility, and it makes the back of Feng's neck prickle. "It is gone. Almost. What remains is not a hook. It is only a scar in the shape of one. But the stair reads blood the way a hound reads a trail, and it is very old and very good, and it found it." He glances over his shoulder at the courier, who has come down behind him with a face like curdled milk. "Release the array, please, and note that the candidate was stopped at seventy-three. Not for failure. For cause."

"Seventy-three," the courier says faintly.

"It is a good mark. I would not call it embarrassing." The inspector turns back to Feng with a slight, dry smile. "Come down with me, Lin Feng, heir of Green Pine Hill. I would like to talk to you. I promise it is not an interrogation. Merely a conversation among colleagues."

"We are not colleagues, sir."

"Not yet." He holds out a hand. "My name is Cheng Yun."

Cheng Yun. Feng goes very still.

He knows the name. Everyone on Green Pine Hill knows it. It was in the Arbiter's letter, and in every council meeting since. An inspector will be assigned. He is in the middle stage of Foundation Establishment. He has the reputation of being honest.

"I was told you were coming to our house," he says slowly.

"In the autumn, if the schedule allows." Cheng Yun's hand is still held out. "I thought I might meet the heir before I met the hill. It saves time."

Feng takes the hand. It is dry and warm and hard with calluses, a writer's hand, a swordsman's hand. He lets the man pull him down the last few steps to level ground.

* * *

They sit in a small stone gatehouse at the foot of the stair, with tea and a plate of honey cakes that Cheng Yun pushes across the table without comment. It is, Feng realizes after a minute, a small room that does not smell of anything. No incense, no ink, no oil. A room that has been swept of everything but its own cleanliness.

"I have to ask you some questions about your house," Cheng Yun says. "You do not have to answer. I would ask only that you do not lie. I will know, and I will think less of you, and I would prefer to like you."

"I do not lie." Feng thinks about that. "Often."

"A good answer." Cheng Yun takes a cake, examines it, and eats half. "Your father is Patriarch. Your grandfather died on the day of a Foundation Establishment attempt, with Zhao Heng at the gate. Your uncle, the steward, was a traitor and was killed. Your hill's vein is dying. Your income has fallen to a third. And in the last year, by the market warden's ledger, the Lin shop has increased its sales of Mirror Guard talismans by a margin that does not fit." He puts the other half down. "Those are not my questions. Those are what I know. I would like to understand why."

"The talismans are better," Feng says.

"They are. I bought one in Willow Ford last month. It held fifty-three breaths against a Qi Refining ninth-stage's palm. A Mirror Guard of that grade is not made by a household that cannot pay its tribute." The inspector's dark eyes do not leave his face. "Who makes the paper?"

Here it is.

Feng has rehearsed this. Father told him, on the road, in an even voice that did not match his words. They will ask about the paper. Old Hu made the machine. Old Hu is the one who understands it. If they ask who taught him, say Old Hu.

"Old Hu," he says. "Our guest elder. An artifact refiner. He built a press and a beater."

"Old Hu." Cheng Yun repeats it without inflection. "A mortal artisan of no rank, according to the Registry. A man who, according to the Arbiter's report, stood in a gate and held off a Foundation cultivator with a bent iron rod."

"He is a very good artisan."

"I have no doubt." A small silence. "Lin Feng. I am going to say something, and I would like you to listen very carefully, because I will not say it again. I do not care how your house makes its paper. I do not care what Old Hu was before he was Old Hu. The Compact has a place for a man who does not wish to be asked. I only care about two things. That the tribute is honestly counted, and that nobody is lying to me about a thing that could get someone killed."

"Killed?"

Cheng Yun sits back. For a moment, the clerk's face drops away, and underneath it is something very tired.

"Do you know why I was on the stair today?" he says. "It is not my duty. I am an inspector of ledgers and deeds. I was there because three of the tributary houses in this valley have sent us a child in the last two years, and none of them is here now."

The tea in Feng's cup has gone cold. "They left?"

"They failed the trial. That is what the Outer Court told their parents. A girl from the river house of Yan, fifteen, double root. A boy from Salt Ridge, fourteen. A boy from Lin Gu's household in the east." He turns the cup in his fingers. "I looked at the trial rolls. Each of them passed the fortieth step. Each of them was entered as a junior disciple. Each of them was last seen alive in the Outer Court residence courtyards. The Court has no record of them leaving. It has no record of them dying. It has, on the page where their names should be, a small clean hole."

The room is very quiet.

"They were all rare roots," Feng says slowly.

"The girl was a dual. The Salt Ridge boy was a triple. The Gu boy was a triple. Not one of them was a failure by any measure the Sect uses." He raises his eyes. "I have a theory. It is a poor one. It has no evidence under it, and it implicates a great many people I would rather not suspect. It is that someone inside the Outer Court has been selling names."

"To whom?"

"To the sort of people who would rather have a gifted child than a ledger." He sets down the cup. "Your left leg has a thread of Blood Qi in it. That is not a coincidence I like. I would be very glad, Lin Feng, if you would keep your eyes open while you are here. And if you hear anything about an urn, I would be glad to hear it too."

"An urn?"

"It is a word I have heard twice in the last year, from two different servants, who each looked over their shoulders when they said it. They would say no more." Cheng Yun's mouth twists. "I did not press them. I should have."

He stands. It is a gentle, ending movement, and Feng stands too, with his heart going hard.

"One more thing," the inspector says, at the door. "The talisman you are carrying in the tube at your neck. I felt it on the stair. A Mirror Guard of a very uncommon sort, with a circuit I have not seen before. I do not ask where you got it. I only suggest that you keep it where it is, and not show it to anyone who does not need to know."

Feng's hand has closed over the tube before he can stop it.

"Yes, sir."

"Good boy." Cheng Yun's voice is dry. "You are the first heir I have met in thirty years who did not try to bribe me. It is a refreshing change."

* * *

The Outer Court is a long, low sprawl of gray roofs on a shelf of the mountain, with a drill ground, an archive, two kitchens, a bathhouse and a hall of residence for each year. Feng is assigned a bunk in a long room with twelve others, the third bed from the door. His chest of belongings is a bundle and a spear. Nobody has told him what to do with the rest of the evening.

He sits on the bunk with the spear across his knees and thinks about stairs.

Seventy-three. He ought to be proud. The attendant at the foot of the stair said it twice, in the tone of a man who has seen a lot of boys come down earlier. A named disciple, with a stipend and a teacher. Nobody has reached seventy in a first attempt for ten years.

He does not feel proud. He feels like something that has been turned inside out and handed back wrong.

"You are the one who got the red ring," says a voice.

He looks up. A boy sits on the next bunk, thin and brown-haired, with a pointed face and quick, sidelong eyes. He cannot be older than fourteen. He has the look of a child who has learned to sleep with one ear open.

"I am Lin Feng."

"Ming. From Salt Ridge." The boy picks at a thread on his blanket. "They say you were stopped for blood."

"A little."

"I knew a boy with blood," Ming says. His voice is very low. "My cousin Wei. He passed the fortieth step last year, with a triple root like you. They put him in the bed where I am sitting. He told me, the second night, that a man came to the window at midnight, a man in a black cloak with a hood, and asked him if he would like to see something. I thought he was making it up."

Feng does not move. "What happened?"

"He went." Ming shrugs, a small, awful movement. "He said he would be right back. That was the last I saw of him." He glances at the door, at the window, at the dark patch of mountain beyond the glass. "They told my uncle he had failed the trial, and gone home. But I was the one who carried his bundle to the gate. He had not gone home. He had not gone anywhere."

"Have you told anyone?"

"I told a man who was asking questions. A thin man in a gray robe. He wrote it down." Ming's eyes are enormous. "Then I thought about it, and I did not sleep. I think the room has a leak. I think someone is listening. I think the window is a door."

"Ming."

"Everyone calls it the urn. I do not know why." He picks at the thread again. "I only know that when a triple root comes through the door, somebody in this courtyard is told."

Feng sets the spear down very slowly on the blanket.

"I am a triple root," he says.

"I know." Ming looks at him with something that is almost pity. "I am sorry."

* * *

The lamps are put out at the ninth bell.

Feng lies on his back in the dark with his hands behind his head. Around him twelve boys breathe, sigh, shift, and settle. The window at the far end of the room is a pale gray square, with the branches of a pine moving slightly against it.

He does not sleep. He is thinking of a kitchen on Green Pine Hill, and a man in a sooty tunic with a bowl of soup, and a small hand pressing a bamboo tube into his own. He is thinking of the ring of fire he put under Old Gou's feet, and the sword that cut a bar of iron, and how little of any of it is going to be any use tonight.

Do not use it unless you really need to.

The pine moves. The window glows. And somewhere in the courtyard, the left leg of Lin Feng begins, very faintly, to burn.

It is not a pressure this time. It is a call. A thin, cold tug below the knee, as though somebody a long way off has laid a finger on a thread that runs through his body, and is pulling it, gently, like a man testing a fishing line.

He turns his head.

At the far end of the room, the window is open. He is certain it was closed. A thin gray shape stands in the gap, a man in a hood, very still, with his hands folded in front of him. The face is a pale blur. It is not looking at the bunks. It is looking, with an unhurried and terrible patience, at the third bed from the door.

On the next bunk, the blanket is flat and empty. Ming is not in it.

Feng's hand closes on the spear. He does not breathe. He does not sit up. He lies in the dark with the line pulling at his leg and a bamboo tube lying cold against his throat, and he thinks, with perfect clarity, in a voice that is not entirely his own:

So this is what you meant, radish.

I really need to.
